edges.description: Loss of hepatic N-oxidation leaves gut-derived TMA unoxidised, so it accumulates systemically and is excreted.
Volatile trimethylamine excreted in urine, breath, sweat, and reproductive fluids produces the characteristic fish-like malodour.
Unoxidised free trimethylamine is excreted in increased amounts in the urine.
Chronic socially stigmatising malodour leads to social isolation and clinical depression.
Severe psychosocial distress from chronic malodour can lead to suicidality and attempted suicide.

nodes.description: Secondary psychosocial consequence of the chronic stigmatising odour rather than a primary neurological feature of the metabolic defect.

evidence.reference_title: Missense mutation in flavin-containing mono-oxygenase 3 gene, FMO3, underlies fish-odour syndrome.
evidence.snippet: The disorder, colloquially known as fish-odour syndrome, is inherited recessively as a defect in hepatic N-oxidation of dietary-derived TMA and cannot be considered benign, as sufferers may display a variety of psychosocial reactions, ranging from social isolation of clinical depression and attempted suicide.

evidence.reference_title: Trimethylaminuria: causes and diagnosis of a socially distressing condition.
evidence.snippet: Because many patients have associated body odours or halitosis, trimethylaminuria sufferers can meet serious difficulties in a social context, leading to other problems such as isolation and depression.

nodes.description: First-line management is dietary restriction of trimethylamine and its precursors—including choline (eggs, liver, kidney, peas, beans, peanuts, soya products, brassicas), lecithin and lecithin-containing fish oil supplements, and trimethylamine N-oxide (marine fish, cephalopods, crustaceans)—as well as FMO3 inhibitors such as indoles (in brassicas) and circumstances that promote sweating. Diet must be monitored to meet daily choline and folate requirements, with no restriction of dietary choline during pregnancy and lactation.

evidence.reference_title: Trimethylaminuria: causes and diagnosis of a socially distressing condition.
evidence.snippet: The symptoms of trimethylaminuria can be improved by changes in the diet to avoid precursors, in particular TMAO which is found in high concentrations in marine fish.

evidence.reference_title: Primary Trimethylaminuria.
evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Foods with a high content of precursors of trimethylamine or inhibitors of FMO3 enzyme activity (seafoods: fish, cephalopods, and crustaceans), eggs, offal, legumes, brassicas, and soya products; food supplements and "health" foods that contain high doses of choline and lecithin; drugs metabolized by the enzyme FMO3; circumstances that promote sweating (e.g., exercise, stress, emotional upsets).

evidence.reference_title: Primary Trimethylaminuria.
evidence.snippet: Planning and monitoring of diet to ensure that the daily intake of choline and folate meets recommendations for age and sex; no restriction of dietary choline during pregnancy and lactation.

evidence.reference_title: Missense mutation in flavin-containing mono-oxygenase 3 gene, FMO3, underlies fish-odour syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Direct sequencing of the coding exons of FMO3 amplified from a patient with fish-odour syndrome identified two missense mutations.

nodes.description: Characteristic body, breath, sweat, and reproductive-fluid odour reminiscent of rotting or decaying fish due to excess excretion of volatile unoxidised trimethylamine. Symptoms are usually present from birth, may worsen during puberty, and in females are exacerbated just before and during menstruation, after oral contraceptive use, and around menopause.

evidence.reference_title: Missense mutation in flavin-containing mono-oxygenase 3 gene, FMO3, underlies fish-odour syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Individuals with primary trimethylaminuria exhibit a body odour reminiscent of rotting fish, due to excessive excretion of trimethylamine (TMA; refs 1-3).

evidence.reference_title: Primary Trimethylaminuria.
evidence.snippet: Primary trimethylaminuria is characterized by a fishy odor resembling that of rotten or decaying fish that results from excess excretion of trimethylamine in the urine, breath, sweat, and reproductive fluids.

evidence.reference_title: Primary Trimethylaminuria.
evidence.snippet: Symptoms are usually present from birth and may worsen during puberty. In females, symptoms are more severe just before and during menstruation, after taking oral contraceptives, and around the time of menopause.

nodes.description: Short intermittent courses of gut-active antibiotics (metronidazole, amoxicillin, and neomycin) suppress TMA production by reducing TMA-generating bacteria in the gut.

evidence.reference_title: Trimethylaminuria: causes and diagnosis of a socially distressing condition.
evidence.snippet: Treatment with antibiotics to control bacteria in the gut, or activated charcoal to sequester TMA, may also be beneficial.

nodes.description: Biallelic loss-of-function FMO3 variants reduce or abolish hepatic flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 activity, the enzyme that catalyses the NADPH- and FAD-dependent N-oxidation of trimethylamine to trimethylamine N-oxide. This is the rate-limiting detoxication step for gut-derived TMA in the liver.

evidence.reference_title: Missense mutation in flavin-containing mono-oxygenase 3 gene, FMO3, underlies fish-odour syndrome.
evidence.snippet: TMA oxidation is catalyzed by flavin-containing mono-oxygenase (FMO; refs 7,8), and tissue localization and functional studies have established FMO3 as the form most likely to be defective in fish-odour syndrome.

evidence.reference_title: The genetic and biochemical basis of trimethylaminuria in an Irish cohort.
evidence.snippet: Inherited trimethylaminuria (TMAU), a rare genetic disorder of hepatic metabolism of trimethylamine (TMA) causing excessive accumulation of malodorous trimethylamine (TMA), is a socially distressing disorder.

evidence.reference_title: Trimethylaminuria: causes and diagnosis of a socially distressing condition.
evidence.snippet: Diagnosis of trimethylaminuria requires the measurement of TMA and TMAO in urine, which should be collected after a high substrate meal in milder or intermittent cases, most simply, a marine-fish meal.

readouts.interpretation: Increased urinary free TMA directly reports systemic TMA accumulation.

evidence.reference_title: The genetic and biochemical basis of trimethylaminuria in an Irish cohort.
evidence.snippet: Genetic testing, sequencing the entire coding region of the FMO3 gene has been recommended for affected individuals who convert less than 90% of the total TMA load to TMAO.

evidence.reference_title: The genetic and biochemical basis of trimethylaminuria in an Irish cohort.
evidence.snippet: Diagnosis is made by biochemical analysis of urine, with the calculation of flavin monooxygenase trimethylamine conversion capacity.

readouts.interpretation: Reduced TMA-to-TMAO conversion is the functional readout of hepatic FMO3 deficiency.

nodes.description: Trimethylamine is generated by the gut microbiota from reduction of dietary precursors including trimethylamine-N-oxide (abundant in marine fish), choline, and carnitine. With hepatic N-oxidation impaired, the free amine accumulates and is excreted unchanged in urine, sweat, saliva, and expired air.

evidence.reference_title: Trimethylaminuria: causes and diagnosis of a socially distressing condition.
evidence.snippet: Trimethylaminuria is a disorder in which the volatile, fish-smelling compound, trimethylamine (TMA) accumulates and is excreted in the urine, but is also found in the sweat and breath of these patients.

evidence.reference_title: Trimethylaminuria: causes and diagnosis of a socially distressing condition.
evidence.snippet: TMA is formed by bacteria in the mammalian gut from reduction of compounds such as trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) and choline.
